questions.q: What is the core architectural difference between a container and a virtual machine?
options: A container shares the host's existing kernel; a VM includes a complete guest OS with its own kernel
A container is always slower than a VM to start
A VM cannot run on a public cloud, only a container can
There is no real architectural difference between them
questions.explain: A VM includes a full guest operating system on top of the hypervisor. A container skips that and shares the host OS's kernel directly.

questions.q: What do Linux namespaces actually do for a container?
options: They limit how much CPU and memory the container can use
They give the container its own isolated view of processes, network interfaces, and mount points
They install a separate kernel for each container
They encrypt the container's network traffic
questions.explain: Namespaces isolate what a container can see — its own PIDs, network interfaces, and mounts — so one container can't see another's processes.

questions.q: What do cgroups do for a container, as distinct from namespaces?
options: They provide isolated visibility into processes and files
They limit how much CPU, memory, and I/O a container is allowed to consume
They are only used in Type 2 hypervisors, not containers
They replace the need for a container runtime like Docker
questions.explain: Cgroups (control groups) cap resource consumption per container, preventing one container from starving others sharing the same host kernel.

questions.q: Why do containers typically start in well under a second, while a VM might take 30 seconds to 2 minutes?
options: Containers use faster physical hardware than VMs
A container just launches a process on an already-running kernel; a VM has to boot an entire OS from scratch
VMs are required to run a virus scan before starting
Containers do not actually run any code until requested
questions.explain: No OS boot is required for a container — it's a process launch on a kernel that's already running, versus a full OS boot sequence for a VM.

questions.q: According to this lesson, when should you choose a VM instead of a container?
options: Whenever you want the fastest possible startup time
When you need a different OS/kernel than the host, or the strongest possible isolation between tenants
Only when running Docker is unavailable
VMs should never be chosen over containers in any scenario
questions.explain: A VM is the right choice when you need a different OS than the host or stronger isolation — containers can't provide a different kernel or the same isolation strength.
